result.topic_en: Formulas for the dip (depression) of the horizon as a function of the eye's height and the Earth's radius, taking terrestrial refraction into account, first with a power-law light path and then with the light path taken as a circular arc.
result.transcription:
Depression des Horizonts $\delta$
Halbmesser der Erde $R$
Höhe des Auges $h$
Amplitudo des Erdbogens $v$
Ganze Refraction $\varepsilon v$
$R+h=r$

$r^{1-\varepsilon}\cos(1-\varepsilon)v = R^{1-\varepsilon}$
$\delta=(1-\varepsilon)v$
Also
$\left(\frac{R+h}{R}\right)^{1-\varepsilon}\cdot\cos\delta = 1$
$2\sin\frac{1}{2}\delta^2 = 1-\left(\frac{R}{R+h}\right)^{1-\varepsilon} = \frac{h}{R}(1-\varepsilon)-\frac{hh}{RR}\frac{(1-\varepsilon)(2-\varepsilon)}{2}$
Nimmt man aber die Bahn des Lichts wie einen Kreisbogen an so ist
$\frac{R+h}{R} = \frac{\cos\frac{2-\varepsilon}{2-2\varepsilon}\cdot\delta}{\cos\frac{\varepsilon}{2-2\varepsilon}\cdot\delta}$

methods.what: Light-path equation in polar form with refraction coefficient (power-law curve) relating the eye's radius, the arc amplitude and the Earth's radius
Dip of the horizon as reduced arc amplitude
Exact relation between dip, height and Earth radius for the power-law light path
Series expansion of the dip to second order in h/R
Dip formula when the light path is taken to be a circular arc

items.quote:
Nimmt man aber die Bahn des Lichts wie einen Kreisbogen an so ist
$\frac{R+h}{R} = \frac{\cos\frac{2-\varepsilon}{2-2\varepsilon}\cdot\delta}{\cos\frac{\varepsilon}{2-2\varepsilon}\cdot\delta}$
items.english: But if one takes the path of light to be a circular arc, then (R+h)/R = cos((2-ε)/(2-2ε)·δ) / cos(ε/(2-2ε)·δ).
